posts.title: Ask HN: Are the trades a safe career transition?
posts.text: I am a software guy. Engineering degree but not PEng. Im thinking of jumping ship because i dont see much of a future in the career. Ai has me a little discouraged I need a few decades of at least mild security to get to retirement... Are the trades safe? Im worried about homeowners and companies ending up with robots that do all those tasks. Not next year obviously, but it could happen before the career change fully pays off And if not the trades, then what is a better bet?

comments.text: If you look at a graph of the US economy, and remove software and data centers, there’s basically no growth. Don’t leave software. AI will change your job, but it won’t replace you, not even in multiple decades. Be strategic about the kinds of software roles you get into. Look for niches with stability. Look to go toward highly regulated software niches. For example, I work in an area where it would be impossible to remove manual testers due to certain regulations. Software work for government where you must be a US citizen or you must do specific things manually could be another example. I also think some areas are going to be more insulated from AI disruption. I think ops and security have more stability. Anything that requires more judgment and less “take inputs and turn them into outputs.” Moving from an upper middle class career track to something you can get into without a high school diploma is a mistake. In many trades you’re competing with dudes who are working under the table and aren’t even documented. Even if you’re not, they’re mostly hard on your body, and some aren’t even immune from automation.
comments.author: Grombobulous

comments.text: I’ve never worked as a professional tradesman, but I’ve done quite a bit of that type of work. It’s hard. It’s hard on your body in ways that will become more of an issue as you age. It’s also, imho, very satisfying work. But it’s tough. And even though you might look at your last plumbing bill and say “damn, that would be good money!” the reality is that very few in the trades will bring all of that home themselves. As for AI in the software field… I’ve watched the people around me. Some of them are doing good work with AI. And what they all have in common is serious skill and experience predating AI. What it looks like from my seat is that AI in software dev and related fields is absolutely a force multiplier… but only for people who already know what they’re doing. So as a few other people have said, don’t be too hasty to jump ship. There may yet be some good opportunities. Btw, having said all of that, my AI use is limited to summarizing searches and assisting on code review. I’m personally quite “anti AI” and close enough to retirement that if eventually I can’t keep up without going all-in, I’m ok with being fired. Love my job and the people I work with, though.
comments.author: allenrb

comments.text: Sorry but your fear about homeowners and companies using robots is just irrational (atleast in your lifetime). A plumber, electrician, carpenter, etc will always be in demand. Humans need real like infrastructure instead of all this stupid digital crap of dubious worth. My wife and I both have graduate degrees. Everyone in my immediate family have graduate degrees. We are all “professionals” in white collar jobs…… and yet I think I’m going to steer my kids into more long term and satisfying careers that work in the physical world.
comments.author: thatonehack

comments.text: Trades are boom bust even more so than software engineering. There is a shortage, people run to the field, but by the time they are trained up (end of apprenticeship) there is probably a bust because there are too many people in them. You need to be prepared to sweat out at least one bust at the beginning of your career, and stay in it so you can reap a boom or two. It’s definitely an exciting time to be in robotics, though it looks like the Chinese are pushing more aggressively into it thsn western developed nations. AI is also a huge risk to the trades (the joke about the plumber just needing to know hit im a call means those quick calls are at risk because that knowledge is easy to get with a chat bot).
comments.author: seanmcdirmid

comments.text: AI is definitely changing things a lot in the field, but don't discount the massive change in how cheap money was during ZIRP and how expensive it became after ZIRP finally ended. This was coincidentally around the same time the layoffs in big tech started, which was before AI really had any meaningful impact. When money is cheap it is a lot easier for companies to hire, and when money suddenly stops being cheap it is a lot harder. In particular, large discontinuities in economic conditions, which we just experienced recently post-covid, always produce downturns in affected industries (which is distinct from the first order aspect of how expensive money is). So I think even ignoring AI we could expect several years of down-ness and reorganization followed by a recovery. I don't think we can even tell this point if AI will reduce demand for developers. The economy for software might be even worse right now if the AI developments hadn't happened when they did, there was an insane hiring spree during COVID and even before that the industry employment-side was growing at a probably unsustainable pace.
comments.author: pfannkuchen

comments.text: Something to keep in mind in these kind of discussions: the most pessimistic visions of the future are not worth preparing for on an individual level even if they end up materializing. This is because apocalyptic problems can only be reasonably addressed with solutions that are very large-scale and political in nature, and trying to minimise your own personal exposure is akin to doomsday prepping. If the doomers are right and AI fully automates knowledge work leaving most unable to produce much value, the entire notion of a 'safe career path' doesn’t make sense. Not just because of robotics, but also because demand for even the safest bets likely collapses in such a scenario. And honestly, in this case there would be far more pressing issues than long term job security. IMO, make decisions like these based on what fulfils you rather than out of fear.
comments.author: gadsdengrappler

comments.text: Safe professions aren't safe. If all knowledge work disappears, you'll live in an economy that's so unstable from high unemployment that it will hardly matter whether your specific chosen profession isn't automated - on the mild end it will affect the demand for what you do, the cost of everything you need to live, your retirement savings, how you get taxed and what your taxes are spent on; on the more extreme end, it won't matter that being a plumber gets you nice house if there people outside throwing bricks through the windows.
comments.author: trio8453

comments.text: My family are all trades people, I went into software. I’m also in a region where trades pay well. Trades are high floor, low ceiling. Initial wages are good, but after journeyman there isn’t much growth. Unless you start your own business, then sky’s the limit. Trades are hard on the body, there’s very little work-life balance, and they are very boom/must cycle dependent. Skilled tradesmen who can mix business acumen are rare, thats where I’d aim for. But for wanting just a “job” software is better and more comfortable. Can always do woodworking in your spare time too.

comments.text: They're making pretty good progress on hands[1,2], I don't have a good sense of how quickly these things will become cheap enough to become ubiquitous, I'd imagine > 5 years but < 10 years. comments.text: Trades are very cyclical and offer little in the way of a safety net. You'll have fat and lean years. The lean years will wipe you out unless you're a phenomenal saver and can keep your lifestyle monk like during the fat years. You will probably be safe from the sort of automation around the corner as the boom is largely contained in the virtual world. There is no such thing as job security in a dynamic economy like ours. The ones who are the most successful are the ones who can stick and move and are unsentimental about what work they are doing.

These are jobs that requires human involvement and advice, and as a homeowner I would much appreciate a human managing these work for me rather than a robot.

posts.title: Ask HN: Tips for transitioning from web development to embedded/firmware?
posts.text: I started my career 15+ years ago doing native development (c, c++, etc), but the last decade I've been doing fullstack web applications. I'd like to transition closer to my roots with a job doing primarily c, c++ or rust. The natural place seems to be in embedded development or firmware work. How feasible is the transition this late in the game? Any advice?

comments.text: Way too much caution in this thread. I've done all kinds of programming including embedded and full stack (from before the latter was even a colloquialized term). I absolutely love the degree of control you can get at the microcontroller level. One of my proudest projects had IRQ handlers written in assembly where I counted instruction cycles in order to guarantee worst-case latencies and well-defined impact to realtime activities in the main loop. There were also some lower-priority tasks going on that were cooperatively multitasked. Some time later I wrote a JavaScript library that mimicked some of those cooperative multitasking concepts to queue background image downloads and other generic "ITasks" in a manner that maximally utilized available connections (which were extremely limited by servers back then) and allowed on-the-fly reordering. The frontend used it to always ensure whatever image the user was most interested in (i.e. tiny previews, and large version of the result presently hovered over or that we anticipate will be hovered next) came up as close to instantaneous as we could get, and the rest of the large images lazy-loaded in an intelligent order. The result was an experience that felt so much faster than how most other websites operated back then (and ironically even now as bloat has really slowed a lot of sites down), and users loved it. So the concepts you learn at one end of the spectrum can definitely benefit you at the other. I have much less fun now that so much of the web has moved to React and other cookie cutter frameworks where the level of control comes at a higher cost (in terms of learning curve, understanding all the layers of abstraction, and space for developer creativity). In other words, just get in there and start playing with a personal project or two, and trust your instincts and all the experience that honed them!
comments.author: rkagerer

comments.text: I'd say just do it. You have been in the industry for 15+ years and you surely know how to network/do interviews. I feel that you are just hesitating or wait for some confirmations. I wrote similar posts so that's my guess, but please criticize me if I'm wrong. My point is, whoever has actually done the transition, their experience may not really help you a lot. They might have a cousin who actually refers them to the company; They might have worked 10 years of embedded projects as a hobby; They might be lucky because 5 years ago there were a huge opening somewhere. I heard of a metaphor about elevators -- Several people ride an elevator to floor 100, and a reporter asked them how they get there -- one of them said he did 1,000 push-ups, another said he read 2 books, and a third said he bumped his head against the elevator's walls. Those experience might be very well relevant, or not. But above all, copying others' experience, in THIS market, probably doesn't work. Now that you are 6 years senior than me regarding SWE experience, I think you already know what to do -- just do it.
comments.author: ferguess_k

comments.text: I started my career in C/C++ and have done a fair amount of embedded work. In terms of actually doing stuff, there has never in the history of the world been a better time to do low-level and embedded systems work. The right advice here: find a project, scrounge the parts, and have an agent do basic bring-up work for you. If your last serious C work was 15 years ago, I think you'll be astonished how quickly you can progress to the "rewarding" part of any project. If your question is instead how you make a career transition to embedded/firmware work, that's much trickier. The obvious concern is AI's impact on the job market, but I'm chiming in to observe that this isn't the biggest problem with a web->embedded transition. Good jobs doing embedded stuff, at least for people who don't already have a pedigree doing that work, has for as long as I can remember been a bottleneck for people wanting to do this stuff. There's simply a lot more high-level work to be done than low-level work. I can see bright spots potentially ahead; I'm not a big Jevon's Paradox person but one kind of clearly Jevon-y area is hardware, because we've zorched one of the biggest impediments to getting new projects off the ground. But it hasn't happened yet, and might not.
comments.author: tptacek

comments.text: For fun or for business? For fun - just do it. There are no barriers. Esp32, audio synthesizer gadget, cameras. Everything is cheap and available. For the money? Expect lower pay, lower standards, worse hours and shit conditions
comments.author: wernam

comments.text: There are two issues: 1) transitioning your skills, and 2) persuading someone to hire/pay you for your new skills. Transitioning your skills is possible. But embedded is a different world and a different mindset. You a lot less RAM and a smaller CPU. You may have hard deadlines - the right answer can be wrong if it's too late. You may have multiple threads that have to share data and not corrupt it, no matter what order events occur in. In the worst case, you may not have logging available at all, and you may not have a debugger. (I think the worst I ever had to do was attach a logic analyzer to the address bus, triggered by a specific address, and then use it to look at past memory addresses in order to figure out what path of execution had got me to the point of the crash.) So, yeah. It's a different world. Learnable, but different. Getting someone to believe you can do it enough that they're willing to pay you: I don't have great advice there. I spent almost my whole career in embedded. It seems to me that it's easier to get from there into, say, desktop programming, than it is to go the other way. Your best bet might be to emphasize your native development background, and count on there being a shortage of embedded people.
comments.author: AnimalMuppet

comments.text: I haven't done much embedded in the past, but LLMs give so much options now to do your own thing. I reverse-engineered all IoT at home and I am currently playing with my 2010 floor heating box. Its dumb but it has ModBus, so can make it more "smart" for remote readings with PicoPi W. I see huge potential in business of reviving old abandonware control software which hardware can't be easily replaced, that may include building new firmwares. Check your personal network and see who may have such old systems running. It may become a job or a business.
comments.author: imhoguy

comments.text: If not embedded, there is still plenty of space for low level PC programming in C/Rust/etc. Try as we might, I don't think we will ever get rid of C as the native language of low level Win/Linux APIs. Someone has to write low level drivers. But embedded is something else entirely that I'd argue is fundamentally incompatible with the perspective of a web dev. In embedded, you need to be aware at every moment of exactly what the CPU is doing and how many resources are being used. You generally don't have multiple CPUs or even threads. Multitasking means hardware interrupts instead of cooperative threads. You also likely need to be aware of assembly because sometimes you have to write a really hot function in raw assembly to get the required performance. Embedded is all about resource optimization, and we dev is about throwing more and more resources at the problem. It will probably be a difficult transition to make because it's a fundamentally different way of looking at and thinking about programming. I would recommend you find a problem, then buy the cheapest microcontroller you can find and spend a few weeks learning how to optimize your code to make maximal use of the hardware while still solving the problem in acceptable time. A big part of getting my current job was talking in my interview about how I solved a novel problem by using an obscure CPU feature in assembly that resulted in 30x fewer instructions than optimized C. Find a problem, solve the hell out of it, and speak confidently about your solution. One benefit that web dev does bring you is thinking about concurrency. Your CPU can only do one thing at a time, but microcontrollers have peripherals that run in parallel, and the embedded system usually consists of multiple chips talking to each other and doing independent work. Managing this concurrency efficiently with a single CPU thread is a large chunk of embedded engineering. Instead of IPC, you do things like set up a DMA pipe between SPI and RAM, trigger an interrupt on I2C bytes, use harhardware timers to simulate threads. You'd be shocked at just how much concurrent work can happen with only a single non-pipelined in-order CPU thread. If you want to break into a new field, the advice is always the same: do the work in your own time, build a portfolio, show you know the job, and speak confidently about the hard problems you learn to solve.
comments.author: unrented7977

comments.text: You can get started learning with any of the amazingly cheap and powerful ESP32, Raspberry Pi, Raspberry Pi Pico, and Arduino stuff out there, along with dirt cheap TANG FPGAs, etc. Get some projects under your belt in your free time. Start with the canonical blinking of an LED, and step it up from there.
comments.author: mikewarot

comments.text: As someone who currently does embedded, and transitioned into it with extremely little professional experience. You need to be able to demonstrate that you understand the tradeoffs that come with embedded and how you can provide value to someone who would hire you. Web development is very much a continuous integration easy to fix bugs kind of environment, in embedded bugs can have real cost. As someone who frequently hopped around across different domains, the key is demonstrating that you understand their problems and can provide value. Also, being curious helps. Also, today with AI am not sure how much native development is going to matter. A handful of best practices in an already set up project plus an AI agent is gonna spit out very workable code. Right now the problem space is very much about reasoning about the larger system, de bugging stuff, thinking about how pieces work together, going in the lab and connecting debuggers so that they agent can do stuff to the hardware, etc.
comments.author: qazxcvbnmlp

comments.text: I see two layers here. One is doing embedded development. The other is getting someone to pay you for it. Embedded development has never had a lower bar to entry. There are cheap development boards, free tools, and modestly priced test equipment. Doing embedded development is entirely up to you. Getting someone to pay for your time doing it is just the generic problem of getting someone to pay for your time doing something you would prefer to do. It depends on other people and your social capital Who you know, how good a hang you are [1], the economics of the field, your opportunity cost and compensation requirements, etc. are what matter most. Luck aside there’s no free lunch. The place to start is your building your network. That’s hard. [1] technical skill might or might not be a determining factor within a workplace culture.
comments.author: brudgers

comments.text: It’s totally doable, as with all things in this industry the bulk of the work is proving you can already do it before someone employs you. Build some toy projects, learn how to use embedded Rust or C, maybe write some blog posts but at the very least have some code on GitHub you can point potential employers at. You’re also going to have to get comfortable with some level of electronics, because it’s very rare someone wants embedded development done that doesn’t interact with the outside world in some way, and that’s going to require knowing how to drive some IO.
comments.author: jon-wood

comments.text: When I went to uni, they had this fun iot course that a company from the area ran as a hiring campaign. Ill brag shamelessly: after the course was over they tried to hire me and I politely declined to keep working in web dev. So maybe find how can you take an iot course in the nearby uni, it might be even free, I feel like this industry is small (at least where I come from) so you can make nice connections, and even if not, well at least you end up with a nice project to show. By the way, this course was hands down the most hardcore thing I ever did. At one point I had to count high pulses for a number of c for loop ticks to read a temperature, in the process of writing the driver by hand (no AI yet), ending up with too high readings, and I couldn't debug it since it's actual pulses of electrons in the wire, once you signal it to start you can't stop it. In the end it was an off by one error, but not the usual kind, I shifted left 1 bit too much. I got stuck like 2 hours in the library trying to figure out what went wrong (I always suspect it's the hw fault, naturally), so that aha moment was really fun! There is something special about creating something physically. I wish you make it soon and have fun!
comments.author: yard2010

comments.text: One of the biggest differences is that in web development you are most of the time oblivious to how things are actually implemented and to the layers underying your software, all the way up to the metal. In embedded, even if you are not working directly with the lower layers of abstraction, it is something you always keep in mind. For example, even if the project uses Linux, with an app written in a higher level language- there are people using Python or even C#- maybe at some point you need to look into the bootloader, and eventually you find yourself reading the reference manual for your SoC to find the boot pins configuration. As to the transition, some time ago I worked with a colleague that had been transferred from another, non-embedded team. I think this is a valid strategy, to join a team with experienced embedded devs. 15+ years of software engineering experience is a lot even if on a different field. On the other hand, on these projects there will likely be some part adjacent to web development, where you can contribute more.
comments.author: jcarrano

comments.text: Stay under ~48V to be touch-safe. Safety squints are not OSHA approved eye protection, get some cheap safeties (and some cheap readers for the little stuff). Clamp motors securely before driving. AI will help a lot, but make sure you work with it on tasks you couldn't do yourself (and then delegate everything you already know to AI). this is a great and easy read, https://www.oreilly.com/library/view/making-embedded-systems... https://github.com/eleciawhite/making-embedded-systems
comments.author: otekengineering

comments.text: IMO the single most important thing about embedded that doesn't exist in web dev is timing assurances. Juggling several competing tasks and making sure each one gets completed at exactly the right time is not an uncommon constraint in this space. My suggestion would be to pick a toy example like motor control or something and use it to learn about state machines.
comments.author: hingler36

comments.text: I've done both over my career (as well as some other stuff.) While they are very different, if you know C, it's not hard to transition. Getting a job in the embedded space though is obviously a lot harder than web. There are simply fewer jobs to be had. Doing some personal projects in the space may reawaken your C skills, and help demonstrate competence. Good luck!
comments.author: bruce511

comments.text: If you have solid foundations and understand how computer systems work, algorithms, data structures, which hopefully is the case from your C years, there should be no problem. Keep in mind "embedded" today is a wide field from small microcontrollers, to embedded systems with virtual memory, to embedded systems running Linux. Back in the day there was a clearer cut, today there are many embedded systems that are very close to your run of the mill "backend" work.There's embedded that's more real-time. There's embedded that's safety critical. Pitch your solid background in C and your "fullstack" web as something that broadened your perspective. Understanding context help everywhere and embedded systems can also have UIs, and some of them even web technology based UIs. Lots of other factors, e.g. your education, what country you're in, and what specific markets you're interested in. There's robotics, there's medical, there's defence, automotive, automation ... lots of options.
comments.author: YZF

comments.text: I just went through that transition myself. My roots are embedded/C++, and I've been moving higher in the stack throughout my career (fullstack web being the latest). I felt like my brain was rotting and wanted to go lower again, and it turns out that good C++ people are really hard to find. If you have legit provable experience there you're going to be golden.
comments.author: kyrofa

comments.text: We have a couple of outstanding embedded developers with decades of experience. Neither of them write a single line of code anymore. Just be realistic about the post AI world, don't fool yourself
comments.author: oivaksef

comments.text: I think if you have a genuine interest in solving problems where that tooling is the best solution, it should be an easy transition. Especially being able to use generative AI as a resource. Now, if you’re just over, focused on technologies and want to use a technology for the sake of using that technology, probably won’t be as easy. Saying you want to transition to C, C++, or Rust is like a handyman saying they want to to get better with electrical tools vs plumbing tools or circular saws vs reciprocating saws. They focus on the problem than try to pick the right tool for the job. Focus on what you want to solve, and then apply the tooling. Solve the same Problems you’ve already been solving, with your new tooling and weigh the pros and cons of both. The obvious choices will come out based on the problem at hand. The jump from web apps to firmware may be a big jump. But if you focus on a problem that interests you, and it appears those techs may be a better tooling for your task. Maybe solve it in your traditional languages first, then re apply the new stack. Or contribute to tools you’re already using, written in those stacks.
comments.author: snailcoder

posts.title: Ask HN: Is a college degree still necessary for a programmer?
posts.text: Hey everyone, I'm currently a second-year university student. I also work part-time as a Backend dev. I did my first internship very early on, in 9th grade. Until then, I worked at three different companies and startups. So to speak, already very experienced in CS. But now that AI is developing so rapidly, I'm a little concerned about my position. Technology is advancing rapidly, and I feel like I won't be able to keep up with it anymore and college takes up a lot of time, too. I'd like to hear your advice on this matter. Thanks for you attention!

comments.text: More than ever. In the past, programmers were just well paid blue collar workers. In the future, we'll see something like proper engineers. Every dev is a systems analyst now. AI is an excellent generalist, but you'll need to know enough to figure out what its trainers haven't. AI companies like to claim AI is being trained by the best minds, but sometimes that skill is latent. It's terrible at creative writing until coached to write properly. It can't do something like Ren'Py well because it doesn't hire any Ren'Py devs for training. The most recent changes make AI lazy, because it saves on cost, but there's also some clear performance reduction. That's where an engineer comes in - you know how the tool works and how to get the most out of it.
comments.author: muzani

comments.text: While bootcamps have been around for a while, and now AI is making writing code significantly more automated, I still feel like college is useful for introducing broadly foundational knowledge like stack vs heap, data structures, etc. from what I’ve observed, many developers who come from bootcamps lack this foundational knowledge and tend to perform worse than other developers. And I still find the foundational knowledge useful day-to-day. I would still recommend going to college for CS personally if you want to work as a professional software developer. Even with AI writing your code, it is still better if the person piloting the AI understands the principles behind the code being generated.
comments.author: vgbm

comments.text: > In Jan 2025, I quit from a mid-size insurance tech company(1000+) after working there for almost 4y, because I was tipped off the they were about to start layoffs and they did. Well, since then I have zero luck finding any job in SWE. I don't know the OP's circumstances. What I am about to say is meant as advice to others and not a criticism of the OP. If you suspect that you may be the target of a layoff, DO NOT SIMPLY QUIT. In this scenario you are a potential liability to your employer. They will almost certainly pay you to leave if they decide to part ways. It is always easier to find a job when you have a job. Maybe you think if there are layoffs and you are retained that it will be a miserable working environment. Fine. DO NOT QUIT. After a round of layoffs you are relatively safe and you can use that time to find another job. It is very likely that layoffs are going to continue as companies restructure because of AI. Have a plan. Keep your wits and hold fast.

comments.text: I had to get back into the industry last year after 4 years off for mental health and caregiving. I was able to get back in - 2 years isn’t that much. But the problem is the front door in hiring is broken. Entirely. I didn’t receive almost ANY replies from hundreds of sent out resumes - I have household names and big public high scale launches and wins on my resume, but no FAANG and no degree. I got 2 job offers. One was through a manager from 8 years prior who was working at a place. One was a recruiter who found me on LinkedIn. I got engagement when someone physically actually knew me, they were actually hiring, and my skills overlapped. My honest advice is to apply places and try that dance, get yourself in front of people, real people, and mainly 1-1. Work everyone you have ever worked with. If you’ve reviewed their PR, they need to know that you need a job. Be kind and genuinely catch up with them if you want to, but they are your PRIMARY resource to get a job and you can’t let shame get in your way. Corporations in general are BROKEN right now in massive ways and the industry is going through a crisis. It will likely become better but whatever you have to do to survive do it. Finally, it seems like solutions architects seem in demand lately, anyone who can help customers with solutions - SWEs can tend to do well if you have some people skills.

comments.text: Something I expect from a senior engineer is the ability to take a failure without placing blame, and turn it into an opportunity to improve things while also taking actions to prevent the same failure mode from occuring. Gaps on resumes are not unique to you. People have unexpected unemployment for many reasons. If you treat that gap like it's a negative thing, and as you say "explain it", I'm going to think there's something negative behind it. Instead treat it as a matter of fact, then present the opportunities you took in the mean time. What makes someone with a gap stand out to is how they "sell" that gap to me. What did you do in that time to improve yourself, keep your skills sharp, grow as a human being? How are you going to show me that you still have passion and drive to remain in this industry? Also, reframe your thinking. You are not an engineer looking for work, you are a sales person selling an engineer. Take time to understand what qualities in an engineer they want beyond mere skills and experience. For example, you don't sell a used car by starting with "It's been on the road 15 years". You try to appeal to what the buyer is looking for. Do they want an easily customizable sports car, a reliable commuter, fuel efficiency? Hiring teams are buyers, you're the product. There's a lot of other boring sounding, but good advice in this thread, such as networking. Networking should not just be about meeting people who may be hiring, it's also about keeping a pulse on the industry and social engagement beyond just talking within online forums. Go to free conferences, meet people, engage. It makes it a lot easier to interview. Whatever you do, don't lie, and I recommend blocking anyone who recommend you do.

comments.text: Things are pretty tough out there. In addition to empathy, let me try to offer some advice as someone observing industry trends from the outside for a while -- especially in the center of the AI insanity that is the Bay Area: The buzzword everyone is looking for is "high-agency." No, not those agents, but yes, those will be essential. Basically employers want someone who will start something from scratch and take it to the finish line all by themselves. So my advice, which others have echoed here: Build something useful -- end-to-end -- from scratch -- with AI -– on your own -- that you can show off as soon as possible. The key point is, "high agency" is by definition not something you can just put on your resume; It is something you show , not tell. Yes, you need to do this even as you go through the absolute hell that is a job search. But trust me, this will a) help get a much better job, and b) help in the long run throughout and beyond your career. This will be the most valuable skill in the near future. A few other thoughts: 0. Get a $100 Pro subscription. Either GPT or Claude, doesn't matter much, but you do want access to Fable or Astra. The volume and variety of things you can get done in that quota is astounding. Codex offers a free quota with Astra if you want to get a sense of things. 1. Target a domain you are already very familiar with. You can draw on your long experience as an engineer, or any personal interests you may have. Say a Math tutoring web app that your students could use. This will sharply cut down the time to MVP. 2. Being an end-to-end thing, this will necessarily be something multi-disciplinary. Think of it as doing a one-person startup, so you're going to be forced to do everythig: design, frontend, backend, infra, and maybe even GTM stuff like marketing. Yes, you may not know most of these things, and obviously won't be great at them, but with AI, everything will be good enough. 3. This conveniently also helps explain the gap in your resume. Nobody needs to know you did this in a few months vs 2 years unless they ask. 4. Even when using AI, keep your hands-on skill warm. Most companies still do old-school leetcode interviews. 5. As an extreme backup this might even become something you monetize yourself. Hope this helps, and all the best!

I mean I get it, impact, interesting work, etc. -- the qualitative measures -- aren't really accounted for, but I'm not looking to make a wholistic comparison. posts.title: Ask HN: Should Uber Ratings Decay over Time?
posts.text: I’ve been thinking about how platforms like Uber calculate reputation scores, and I believe there’s a fundamental flaw in how historical ratings are treated. Uber calculates passenger ratings using the last 500 rated trips, regardless of when those trips occurred. In my case, I have 455 ratings, 426 of which are five stars (93.6%). My overall rating is 4.86. What bothers me isn’t the score itself, but the underlying methodology. A negative rating from five years ago can carry exactly the same weight as one received yesterday. And if you’re an infrequent user who hasn’t accumulated 500 ratings, that negative feedback could influence your reputation for years. This raises an interesting question: Should reputation systems measure your historical average, or should they attempt to represent who you are today? One possible solution is exponential time decay: Weight = 2^(-t/H) Where t is the age of the rating and H is a half-life, perhaps 12 months. Under that approach, a rating from one year ago would carry 50% of its original weight, and one from two years ago just 25%. Of course, this introduces other challenges. How do you prevent someone with a history of poor behaviour from simply waiting for their reputation to recover? How do you maintain statistical confidence for infrequent users? Would Bayesian smoothing or a minimum effective sample size help? There’s also a broader philosophical question around the right to be forgotten. Should digital reputation systems indefinitely preserve the consequences of historical assessments, particularly when those assessments are subjective and potentially no longer representative? I’m curious how others would approach this. * Is a rolling window of 500 ratings statistically defensible without considering time? * Would exponential decay produce a fairer and more predictive reputation score? * Should platforms expose both a lifetime rating and a recent-behaviour rating? * Are there better approaches already being used in other reputation systems? I’d be particularly interested in perspectives from people who’ve worked on marketplace ranking, trust and safety, or reputation algorithms. It seems like a relatively simple mathematical change, but one with potentially significant implications for fairness across digital platforms.

comments.text: The reasoning ability is not what is missing. Claude could very easily deduce that it needs to walk to the other room, pick and object up and bring it back based on the prompt. The difficulty is then mapping that goal of "move to other room, grab, move back" to actual outputs to some motor system. And "pick up object" is much too complex to be compared to a simple tool call in some AI agent. It is one thing for an LLM to understand when it needs to run a bash script to collect some system info. It is another thing entirely to expect it to be able to take an image, process it, understand depth/distance, map that delta to some co-ordinate system, then call the exact correct motor functions with the right parameters to cover that distance, ( not accounting for positioning hand to correctly grip and pickup the object of arbitrary shape) grab the item and return home. Doing this using traditional preset instructions and training data is not impossible, but if you mean a truly dynamic AI driven robot, there is just so much variance we arent at a point where it can be consistently producing realistic/desired results (commercially of course.) though I don't think we are very far from it. TLDR, agentic AI for programming today is still leaps and bounds behind a consistent realistic AI body. Many many many moving pieces where the hallucinations and variance in modern LLMs largely produces inconsistent results. I am not an expert, this is just from anecdotal experience working with very simple robotics and LLMs.

Now that one person can do the job of 5, AND there will be an increased demand for more developers from more businesses popping up, we'll be paid a hell of a lot more for the value we can generate. And so it goes, more and more specific desires, with fewer and fewer people that want those specific desires. So one possible future is that we move further out on the fractal. More people get what they want, even if not many people want the same thing. This means that the customizations have to take less software engineer time, because a customer base of just a few people can't pay very much. In that future, the key activity is going to be efficiently finding small groups of users, learning what they actually want, and then generating that.

There will be little to no working knowledge of the internals of large applications and these employers will bleed money on outside consultants to occasionally provide manual maintenance and security hot fixes. Everything will continue to look good from the outside, but really its a messy house of cards. Silo 2 - This will be institutional shops of skilled experts. Game companies that own internally developed rendering engines, kernel developers, independent open source, and systems architects come to mind. These will be people that might occasionally dabble in AI for various things, but they manually modify their code. These are experts who do not gain productivity by offloading their greatest challenges to AI. Silo 3 - The consulting class. This is where the money will be. Technology design firms already do most of this, but the problems these consultants solve for their clients will be greater and the clients will be less capable. These people will explode in demand, but supply will likely remain unchanged, because experts are hard to grow and the corporate world won't produce them. --- I also predict the job recruitment industry will struggle as demand for talent stratifies, because software as an industry struggles to identify talent. This problem will remain unsolved until something catastrophic happens and most employers need to simultaneously unload liability in ways they are currently forced to accept it internally. posts.title: Ask HN: Why no AI-led memory vulns in Python?
posts.text: Python usually means CPython, which means C. Most AI-led vulnerabilities lately have been memory mismanagement - what is keeping Python isolated if it is written in C?

comments.text: Well, it might just be a matter of time. We've already had serious issues in Ruby with both string case conversion ( https://verialabs.com/ruby2shell/ ) and the regex engine (e.g. https://www.ruby-lang.org/en/news/2026/10/23/regexp-fixes-fo... ). And there have been attempts at fuzzing Python that have found real issues, apparently just not on the same scale (e.g. https://github.com/Broyojo/python-formalization ). A couple of things I can think of: first, the model for interfacing to "compiled code" — both C extensions, and compiled Python bytecode — isn't expected to be secure anyway, and never has been. You can trivially wrap a garbage `bytes` in a `code` object, execute it and get a segfault; and you can trivially use the `ctypes` API to corrupt memory. Second, the normal use paths are well-tested and bottom out in an interpretation layer that isn't very well optimized because of how much dynamic nonsense it has to support (even beyond other languages in its class like Ruby). On the other hand, the bytecode format tends to change with almost every "minor" release (i.e. annually now). There's probably plenty of room for a mistake in that churn.
